1: Welcome the group. Frame the session: candidates are one half of every placement, and most deals that fall over do so because of something we didn’t find out on the first call. By the end of today everyone should be able to run a structured, compliant qualification call, lock in representation, and run outbound across LinkedIn, Recruiter and SourceWhale. Ask: who made a candidate call this morning? What’s the one question you always ask?
2: Walk through the three outcomes. Check everyone brought a live role, the exercise later uses it. Timing: 5 minutes.
3: This is the spine of every candidate call. Same order, every time, so nothing gets missed. Emphasise step 2: motivation is the single best predictor of whether a candidate will accept, if you can’t write down their push and pull factors after the call, you haven’t qualified them. Step 4 is desk-specific: each team lead should give trainees their five domain questions (e.g. SWE: stack, scale, system design ownership; Energy: project types, licensing; GTM: quota, attainment, deal size). Step 7: never end a call without proposed interview availability, e.g. “Monday 9–12 or Wednesday 3–5”. Timing: 10 minutes.
4: Go column by column. Motivation questions tell you whether this candidate will actually move. Logistics questions stop late-stage surprises, note the wording: we ask for TARGET package, not current salary, and we ask about work authorisation and sponsorship, not citizenship or visa type (next slide explains why). Network questions turn every candidate call into business development: manager names become BD leads, competing processes tell you who is hiring. Log everything as pre-screen notes in Bullhorn and add the candidate to the right hotlist. Timing: 10 minutes.
5: This replaces the old checklist that asked for current salary and listed citizen / green card / TN / H-1B / OPT. Explain plainly: NYC’s salary history law (and similar laws in many states) bars asking about pay history; federal anti-discrimination rules mean we shouldn’t ask about citizenship or visa category, the two compliant questions are authorisation to work and need for sponsorship. Target package gives us everything we need to submit at the right number. This is not legal advice, if in doubt, check with your manager or HR before asking. Have trainees rephrase three “don’t ask” questions aloud. Timing: 5 minutes.
6: Representation protects the deal: without written confirmation, a duplicate submission from another agency can cost us the fee. The old template named one client in the email and another in the pitch, always check [Client] is consistent throughout before sending. Send within the hour while the call is fresh, and follow up with a text so it doesn’t sit in their inbox. Don’t over-sell the timeline: say what will happen and when you’ll next be in touch, then do exactly that. Timing: 5 minutes.
7: The pitch pack goes underneath the representation email. Candidates are wary of being sold to by recruiters, but well-researched facts about the product, founders, funding and press are persuasive on their own. Merge is shown as a worked example of the structure: build one for each of your clients, refresh the funding and press lines every quarter, and save it in the shared drive so the whole team can reuse it. Check every fact against the client’s own site before sending, and keep the client name consistent throughout: the old template named one company in the email and a different one in the brief. Timing: 5 minutes.
8: Every team sources differently: engineering desks lean on LinkedIn and meetups, Evergreen relies more on cold calling and industry events, and contract desks lean on hotlists and referrals. Run the question at the bottom as a quick round-the-room. The aim is for every consultant to commit to adding one new channel this month. The best candidates are usually passive, so direct outreach should make up most of your sourcing time.
9: LinkedIn is the volume channel. Once someone accepts, messaging is free, so the connection itself is the asset. The opening message should be short, specific and personal: name the project, the stack or the company, never “your impressive background”. The four levers to test are length, directness, tone and specificity; change one at a time so you know what made the difference. Ask the room to share their best-performing connect note. Remind them to tag MVPs: they are the people you keep warm with market updates even when you don’t have a role for them. Timing: 6 minutes.
10: The downside of Recruiter is cost: one message is one credit. So InMail is the precision tool, for the profiles you most want to speak to. The template has three jobs: show why you picked them (the specific match), give enough about the company to spark interest (hyperlink the pitch pack rather than pasting it), and make a small ask. Encourage people to run a generic version and a direct version side by side for a week and compare reply rates with their manager. If a team member has a strong live example with a good response rate, show it here. Timing: 5 minutes.
11: SourceWhale is the most credit-efficient way to run multi-touch outreach: one credit covers a whole 3–10 step sequence. The best candidates in the market are usually passive, so most won’t reply to step 1. Each step should add something new: the role, then proof (funding, a launch), then a market insight, then a polite break-up. The break-up email often gets the highest reply rate because it is low-pressure. Spacing is a guide: adjust to your market. Ask each consultant to build one four-step sequence for a live role before the end of the week and review it with their manager. Timing: 6 minutes.
12: Deeper thoughts, quicker wins. Most consultants read a profile for the one role they are working on and move on. The best treat every profile as a map: past employers give you target companies, their leaders give you business development leads, and a layoff tells you a whole team may be on the market. Run a live example here: open a real profile on screen and ask the room to call out every lead they can find in two minutes. Remind everyone to hotlist the companies in the CRM so the whole team benefits. Timing: 8 minutes including the live example.
13: Prepare the candidate briefs in advance: a name, current role, push and pull factors, and one hidden deal-breaker (for example, a holiday booked in three weeks, a competing final-stage interview, or a hybrid requirement the role can’t meet). The caller’s job is to find it. Observers score four things: did they uncover genuine motivation, did they handle logistics compliantly (target package, not current salary; authorisation and sponsorship, not visa type), did they find the deal-breaker, and did they book a next step. Keep feedback structured: one thing that worked, one thing to change. Timing: 25 minutes.
14: Give everyone two minutes to write their own three takeaways before showing this slide, then compare. Each action should land on the desk this week, and managers should follow up: book the paired role-play, and review InMail open and reply rates together the following week. Ask each person to say out loud which action they will do first. Timing: 5 minutes.
15: Open the floor for questions. Close by linking forward: today was the candidate half of the placement; the next module covers the client half, starting with qualifying the job properly so every candidate call you make is aimed at a role that can actually be filled.
